**How it works:** Instead of creating a fresh connection each time you query, a pool maintains N idle connections (configured size). Requests grab one, use it, return it. New connections only created up to the limit; excess requests wait briefly for a free one.

**Why it helps:**

Creating a connection is expensive—handshake, authentication, memory setup. At scale, app → DB latency dominates query time. Reusing connections amortizes that cost across hundreds of requests.

**Resource cap:** Pool bounds connections, preventing exhaustion (each connection holds memory, file handles, threads on the server). Without pooling, 1000 concurrent users = 1000 DB connections; with pooling of 20, same users reuse the 20 connections.

**Latency cliff avoided:** New connection per request → *every* request pays connection cost → P99 latency spikes under load. Pooled → grab-and-go, consistent microseconds.

**DB stability:** Limits concurrent sessions on the server, preventing it from being hammered into saturation.

Tradeoff: stale connections (timeout after idle N minutes) need eviction/refresh; misconfigured pool size (too small → queue backups, too large → waste) hurts. But the win—10-100x latency drop under load—is why every production app uses one.
